name: Curtained hair

lead: Curtained hair is a style in which the fringe is parted down the middle (or slightly off-centre) and falls to either side of the face, usually with shorter sides and back. People wear it to frame the face, draw attention to the eyes and cheekbones and add soft symmetry.

The look has a long history, from artist Aubrey Beardsley in the late 19th century to working-class British youth subcultures, the 1990s and K-pop idols. Styling guides describe it as suiting many face shapes, though no research tests how it affects perceived attractiveness.

paras: It is grown out on top to roughly brow-to-cheekbone length, parted in the centre and styled with a blow-dry or light product so each side falls away from the forehead. Men often pair it with tapered or clipped sides; women's version is usually curtain bangs blended into longer layers. Straight and wavy hair sit most easily, with curly hair adjusted by layering.

There are no health risks beyond the usual ones of heat styling and products. Style guides note that the look depends on hair density and growth pattern at the hairline, so thin or receding hairlines can change how the fringe falls.

angle.text: The cut changes how the face is framed immediately, drawing the eye to the centre of the face and covering part of the forehead. People choose it to soften angles or add a youthful, textured look.

lead: Curtained hair, also called curtains, is a hairstyle with a long fringe parted in the middle or to the side, with short or shaved sides and back [1]. The two halves of the fringe fall symmetrically on each side of the face like curtains.

People use it as a face-framing style. Styling descriptions say it softens angular features, draws the eye to the eyes and cheekbones and adds symmetry and a relaxed, textured look [2]. It is distinguished from side-swept bangs, which sweep the fringe all to one side, and from the shag, which has layering throughout [2].

The style has recurred in fashion. Wikipedia traces short, curtained hair to the Baiyue people of modern Vietnam in the first millennium BCE, artist Aubrey Beardsley in the late 19th century, and Glasgow Neds, Manchester Scuttlers and Birmingham Peaky Blinders in the early 20th century [1]. A centre-parted variant returned among new wave and synthpop fans in the late 1980s and was worn by actor Brendan Fraser in the 1990s; it is also associated with K-pop artists [1].

paras: The style is built on a long fringe, commonly four to eight inches, parted down the middle so it falls from the eyebrows toward the cheekbones or beyond [2]. For men it is paired with shorter, tapered or clipped sides and back; for women it appears as curtain bangs blended into bobs, long bobs or long hair [2].
Length changes the effect: a brow-grazing fringe is subtle, a mid-cheek fringe frames more dramatically and a jaw-length one blends into the rest of the hair [2].

Wikipedia notes the early 20th-century longer undercut variant among working-class young men and street gangs, held with paraffin wax in interwar Glasgow, and the late 1980s centre-parted revival derived from the bowl cut [1]. Grokipedia describes a 1970s rock-star revival, a 1990s grunge and Britpop boom and later versions worn by celebrities and by women through curtain bangs, a style attributed to Brigitte Bardot in the 1950s [2]. These accounts differ in detail and reflect fashion histories rather than dated studies.

Style descriptions say the cut flatters oval and heart-shaped faces and can soften square or round ones, and that straight or wavy hair is the easiest texture, with curly hair needing adjusted layering [2]. Maintenance is described as low, with regular trims and light products.

Looksmaxxing communities discuss curtains and related middle-part cuts as a low-cost way to frame the face, and sometimes as a way to soften a high forehead or a wide face. It overlaps with the entry on middle part and textured crop trends.
